messages.author: 4a9d3cdb4d9390f0
messages.subject: Camera trap data
parts:
Hi again, thank you for your help with my last question! 
I have two more, which I hope are not too basic but I am having a hard time finding the answers myself.
First of all, if I am working with data from camera-traps, do I need to include the cameras which did not take any pictures in my data set? I assumed not, as a person-observer would also only note the events in which he did see something, but maybe I`m approaching it wrong. 

Also, I have created all my models in the software and the functions seem to be okay, but the density estimates I get so far are still very low, much lower than estimates obtained from the same data with the random encounter model. I also recreated everything in R and if I understand correctly in the papers I found, besides area size and sampling effort, I also need to use the detection angle of the camera as a multiplier to get density and abundance estimates. Is it also possible to include this 42° angle as a multiplier in the software, to get more accurate results or does this rather work in R? 

Thank you very much, 
Carolin Klangwald

messages.author: 2d63935e6f128a26
messages.subject: Re: Camera trap data
parts:
Hi Carolyn,

Yes, you need to include the cameras which did not take pictures if they were working and could have detected animals. Add one row for each camera with the information about sampling effort at that point (as would be the case if a person observer visited a point and didn't see anything), and put "NA" in the distance column. 

Yes, you can use a multiplier to account for the fact that CTs monitor a sector that is only a small fraction of a circle, and yes, otherwise your estimates will be much too low. For an AOV of 42 degrees, I used a multiplier of 0.1166667 which would inflate the estimate by a factor of  1 / 0.11666667  =  8.57. See here for an example in R: https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html 

You could alternatively include the sampling fraction in the "Effort" at each point, calculated as theta * Tk / 2*pi*t following Howe et al (2017), where theta of 42 degrees = 0.733 radians. 42 of 330 degrees is the same as 0.733 of 2*pi radians, and describes the portion of a circle your cameras monitored.

All the best,
Eric

messages.subject: Re: Camera trap data
parts:
Hi Eric,

But in your example (https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html), you also defined the sample fraction as an object:
viewangle <- 42 # degrees
samfrac <- viewangle / 360

and the object "samfrac" was later used in the function (e.g. dht2 or bootdht).
So it is necessary to include the column "multiplier" in the initial data frame as you included in "DuikerCameraTraps", and additionally create the object "samfrac"?

Or would it be enough to define the object "samfrac"?

Thank you so much
Best
Pablo
